title: Could Oracle Actually Achieve 120% Upside? Or Is Cantor Fitzgerald Totally Wrong?

Could Oracle Actually Achieve 120% Upside? Or Is Cantor Fitzgerald Totally Wrong? ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Oracle stock has lost 53% over the past year, and Cantor Fitzgerald reiterated its Overweight rating and $284 target on Oct. 22, 120% up from yesterday's close.

The slide comes from how Oracle is paying for its AI buildout: negative free cash flow, more debt, a $20 billion stock sale and a backlog that leans on OpenAI.

Analysts' earnings estimates have edged up over the past 90 days, to $8.14 a share for the year ending May 2027 and $11.00 for the year after.

Cantor's target implies 33x forward earnings, well above Oracle's 21x five-year average, so the call seems…a little stretched. I'm not buying it.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) has lost 53% over the past year, and Cantor Fitzgerald thinks it can get it all back and then some.

On Oct. 22, Cantor analyst Thomas Blakey reiterated his Overweight rating and $284 price target, 120% above Oracle's $129.10 close on Oct. 21.

Investors balked at the bill

The slide picked up in June, when Oracle said it planned to raise $40 billion of debt and equity in fiscal 2027, after negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026.

In its first-quarter report on Sept. 10, capital spending hit $28.5 billion, free cash flow was negative $5 billion, and Oracle finished selling $20 billion of new stock. On when free cash flow turns positive, CFO Hilary Maxson said on the call: "We haven't given a particular time frame on that yet, and we don't expect to give that today."

Then Oracle sank 9% on hot inflation data last week, and Steve Eisman argued that half of Oracle's backlog is OpenAI.

Cantor hasn't budged

Cantor has held its $284 target since raising it from $229 in early June. It sees Oracle as a key beneficiary of AI spending.

Most analysts agree: 28 Buys and 7 Outperforms against 7 Holds and one Sell, up from 19 Buys in August 2025.

Does $284 add up?

Analysts have cut targets even as they've turned more bullish. The consensus target has come down from $350 a year ago to $237, its lowest point of the year…

Oracle (ORCL): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

Individual targets now run from $110 to $400.

Earnings estimates are holding up. Analysts expect normalized EPS of $8.14 for the year ending May 2027, in line with Oracle's $8.10 guidance, and $11.00 the year after…

Oracle (ORCL): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024–2028 (years to May) (TIKR)

Both have edged up over the past 90 days, from $8.05 and $10.89, while the stock fell. And September's raised guidance gives no reason to expect cuts.

title: Where Will Oracle Stock Be in 2029?
detail:
Where Will Oracle Stock Be in 2029?
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool

ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) should ideally have been one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom, but a closer look at the company's stock price performance suggests that hasn't been the case so far.

Oracle stock has dipped 53% over the past year. The company has been taking on significant debt to fund the aggressive build-out of data center capacity to fulfill the massive contractual backlog it is carrying. The ballooning debt has caused panic among investors. However, we will look past the noise and check if Oracle can prove the naysayers wrong and head higher over the next three years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Oracle's debt is a concern, but investors shouldn't miss the bigger picture

Oracle has a debt of just over $169 billion, according to Yahoo! Finance. That's significantly higher than its $37 billion cash pile. Moreover, the company's aggressive capital spending has dented its free cash flow.

ORCL Free Cash Flow data by YCharts

So, it is easy to see why investors have been spooked about Oracle's prospects, especially at a time when interest rates are rising, inflation is hotter-than-expected, and there are concerns about whether AI infrastructure companies will get access to capital amid high borrowing costs. However, that's one way to look at things.

The reason why Oracle has been ramping up capex and is taking on debt is that it wants to quickly convert its sizable contractual backlog into revenue. The company reported $664 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO) at the end of the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (ending Aug. 31, 2026).

The metric, which refers to the total value of a company's unfulfilled contracts at the end of a quarter, increased by $209 billion from the year-ago period. Notably, Oracle's infrastructure build-out efforts are accelerating growth. It reported a 30% year-over-year increase in revenue in fiscal Q1 to $19.3 billion, driven by a 121% spike in cloud infrastructure revenue to $7.4 billion. That was a solid improvement over the 12% revenue growth Oracle clocked in the same period last year.

Additionally, Oracle's non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) growth rate also jumped from 6% in the year-ago period to 30% last quarter. Looking ahead, Oracle's growth is poised to continue accelerating, as the company is receiving more contracts than it can fulfill. For instance, Oracle booked over $30 billion in contracts for its cloud AI services last quarter, well above the revenue it generated during the quarter.

title: Is IBM Worth Buying as Software Growth Meets a Premium Valuation?
detail:
Is IBM Worth Buying as Software Growth Meets a Premium Valuation?
Supriyo Bose
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 7:08 AM MST 3 min read
IBM
MSFT
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

International Business Machines Corporation IBM is showing better software execution, stronger cash generation and improving profitability, but the stock already trades above its own longer-term valuation norm. That creates a more demanding setup for new buyers.

Recurring software revenues and AI-related opportunities support the growth case. Yet modest Consulting growth, elevated debt and mixed Zacks Style Scores suggest investors still have reasons to remain selective.

IBM Software Growth Strengthens the Bull Case

Software revenues increased 9% year over year at constant currency in the third quarter of 2026. Red Hat grew 11%, Data advanced 20% and Transaction Processing rebounded 10%. Annual recurring revenue rose 8% to $24.9 billion, adding durability to IBM's software-led strategy.

Management now expects Software revenues to grow 7%-8% in 2026, with double-digit Hybrid Cloud growth and mid-teens Data growth. The competitive backdrop remains intense. Microsoft Corporation MSFT reported 43% growth in Azure and other cloud services in its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, while Oracle Corporation ORCL posted 120% constant-currency growth in cloud infrastructure revenues in its fiscal first quarter of 2027. Those results underscore the pace of enterprise cloud and AI investment IBM must keep addressing.

IBM's Cash Flow Offers Financial Support

IBM generated $7.8 billion of free cash flow through the first nine months of 2026, up $600 million year over year. Management raised its full-year expectation and now projects free cash flow growth of more than $1 billion from 2025.

That cash generation provides room to fund operations, dividends and strategic investment while absorbing acquisition-related demands. IBM returned $4.8 billion to shareholders through dividends during the first nine months and ended September with $11.1 billion in cash, restricted cash and marketable securities.

IBM Still Faces an AI Monetization Challenge

Generative AI represented about 30% of Consulting revenues and 35% of Consulting backlog in the third quarter. The trailing 12-month book-to-bill ratio remained above 1.0, indicating continued demand for transformation work.

Revenue conversion remains less convincing. Consulting revenues grew only 2% at constant currency, and segment profit margin declined modestly as IBM reinvested productivity gains into digital assets and its Services-as-Software model. Management still expects low-to-mid-single-digit Consulting growth for 2026, making profitable conversion of the AI backlog an important test.

title: IBM Is Up 11.1% in Three Months. Can Its Momentum Keep Building Now?

Trading disclosure

International Business Machines Corporation IBM shares have gained 11.1% in the past three months, putting the focus on whether better operating execution can support further upside.

The third quarter strengthened that case, with faster Software growth, improved transaction execution and wider operating margins. Still, uneven enterprise spending, mainframe cycles and a valuation above IBM's historical median keep the setup balanced.

IBM's Three-Month Gain Meets Stronger Execution

IBM's third-quarter revenue growth accelerated to 6% at constant currency, while operating earnings per share increased 11% year over year. Operating pretax margin expanded 70 basis points, reflecting productivity actions and better execution across the portfolio.

The quarter also showed improvement in areas that had raised timing concerns earlier in the year. Transaction Processing grew 10% and Infrastructure advanced 5% at constant currency. Yet mainframe-related demand can be cyclical, so sustaining the stock's recent gain will require continued execution beyond a single quarter.

IBM Software Growth Adds Fundamental Support

Software revenues increased 9% at constant currency. Red Hat grew 11%, Data advanced 20% and annual recurring revenue climbed 8% to $24.9 billion, giving IBM a larger recurring-revenue base to support its software-led strategy.

The competitive backdrop remains demanding. Microsoft Corporation MSFT reported 43% growth in Azure and other cloud services in its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, showing the scale of enterprise cloud demand. Oracle Corporation ORCL posted 120% constant-currency growth in cloud infrastructure revenues in its fiscal first quarter of 2027, highlighting the pace of AI-related infrastructure expansion.

IBM's Consulting AI Backlog Is Still a Test

Generative AI represented about 35% of IBM Consulting backlog and 30% of segment revenues in the third quarter. That points to meaningful enterprise engagement as clients modernize applications, data foundations and workflows for AI.

Monetization remains the key test. Consulting revenues rose only 2% at constant currency, and segment profit margin declined modestly as IBM reinvested productivity gains into digital assets. Faster revenue conversion and profitable delivery would make the AI backlog a more visible contributor to the growth story.

IBM Valuation Could Cap Further Upside

IBM trades at 19.3X forward 12-month earnings, above its five-year median of 17.3X. The multiple is also close to the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's 19.8X and the S&P 500's 19.5X.

That valuation leaves less room for execution setbacks. Software growth, Consulting acceleration and margin expansion will need to remain on track for the stock to justify a sustained premium to its own historical norm.

Investors holding Docusign (DOCU) likely still remember the stock's high in September 2021. Shares closed on October 21, 2026, resting 73.7% below that level. It is easy to measure every new rally against that old price, treating the previous peak as the natural home for Docusign stock. So how big a gain would getting back actually take?

Docusign Stock Needs A 280.5% Gain To Get Back

Docusign stock needs a 280.5% gain to recover from its 73.7% deficit and reach its former high. Even if that recovery took three years, it would require an annual return of 56.1%. A shareholder waiting for the old price is counting on exactly that climb.

Has Docusign Stock Ever Gained 280.5% In Three Years?

It has, but not often. Look at every three-year window of Docusign trading since April 2018. Each stretch spans 756 trading sessions, with a new period beginning on every single trading day. These stretches overlap, so one long climb can count in many of them. The stock gained 280.5% or more in 11.6% of those overlapping periods. Returning to its old high within three years will require Docusign stock to pull off a rare feat.

What Has Waiting Cost Docusign Holders?

The wait has now lasted 5.1 years since that peak in September 2021. Over those years, Docusign stock is down 73.7% while the S&P 500 is up 71.0%. Both figures are before dividends. The cost of waiting involves both the direct loss in Docusign and the missed gains that the same capital would have earned in the broader index.

Is Docusign The Same Business It Was Then?

Docusign operates a larger business today than it did at its high, and the company is now profitable.

Revenue for the twelve months through July 2026 stood 87.3% higher than in the twelve months before the high. Over that same stretch, Docusign shifted from an operating loss equal to 5.9% of revenue to an operating margin of 12.0%. The company continues to sell eSign, which management called the premium product in its category on the September 3, 2026 call. It also sells IAM, a platform for managing agreements that management said is an increasingly meaningful part of the business.

The stock traded for 28.1 times its sales at the end of September 2021, weeks after the high. Back then, revenue had expanded 54.2% over a single year, compared with 8.6% in the latest twelve months. Investors paid that multiple for growth that has since slowed, so the price back then was the unusual part.

Bloom Energy Gains as Oracle's 2.8 GW Deal and $25 Billion Brookfield Pact Set a High Bar ©Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Bloom Energy rose 7.1% to $239 on October 21, a day before Q3 results due after the close.

Q2 revenue hit $1.065 billion, up 166%, and 2026 guidance rose to $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion.

That guide requires $2.08 billion to $2.38 billion of second-half revenue, with the stock at 67.0x forward earnings.

Today's report should show whether Oracle deliveries and the roughly 34% gross margin target are holding.

Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) heads into Q3 with a stock that already assumes a great deal. Shares jumped 7.1% to $239 on October 21, a day before results.

It's been a wild year. Bloom joined the S&P 500 in September, and the stock ranged from $76 to $351 over the past 12 months. It now sits about 32% below that peak.

The setup is simple. Bloom raised its 2026 outlook in July, so Q3 is where investors find out whether the back half is actually showing up.

The billion-dollar quarter

Q2 gave Bloom its first quarter above $1 billion in sales.

Revenue rose 166% to $1.065 billion, with product revenue up 215% to $935.4 million.

Non-GAAP gross margin climbed 604 basis points to 34.3%.

Operating cash flow swung to $226.4 million from a $213.1 million outflow.

Management raised 2026 revenue guidance to $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion from $3.4 billion to $3.8 billion. It kept roughly 34% non-GAAP gross margin and lifted non-GAAP operating income guidance to $800 million to $900 million.

CFO Simon Edwards called it "another record quarter for Bloom" on the earnings call, crediting data-center deliveries.

The top line has turned sharply.

Bloom Energy (BE): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2027 (TIKR)

The midpoint of the new guide implies revenue doubling in 2026, so delivery timing now matters more than demand.

Oracle and Brookfield fill the funnel

Two agreements anchor the demand story. Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) expanded its deal to as much as 2.8 GW of Bloom fuel cells, with an initial 1.2 GW contracted and deploying across U.S. projects. Up to 2.45 GW could go to Project Jupiter in New Mexico.

Brookfield Asset Management (BAM) then expanded its AI power partnership with Bloom fivefold, from $5 billion to $25 billion. That gives customers a way to get fast power without paying for it upfront.

Neither figure is booked revenue. Bloom still has to turn both frameworks into delivered systems.

Speed is the pitch. Grid interconnections can take years, while Bloom installs on-site power far faster, and that gap supports pricing.

Do margins back that up?

Bloom Energy (BE): gross margin (%), quarterly, Q2 2024–Q2 2026 (TIKR)

Trailing gross margin sits at 31.7%, below Q2's 34.3% non-GAAP pace, which suggests mix is still improving.

Over the five years to October 20, 2026, one stock outperformed 117 of the 125 other companies in its industry. That stock is Strategy (MSTR), the bitcoin treasury company formerly known as MicroStrategy, and its industry is Application Software. Before sizing a position on that record, an investor should understand where the gain originated. So was it the industry Strategy sits in, or Strategy itself?

How Far Strategy Is Ahead Of Its Industry

Shares of Strategy rose 88.2% over those five years, while the typical Application Software company fell 46.1%. The table below displays figures for the median company across the industry, sector and all-stock groups, alongside the S&P 500 index.

While a position in the typical software stock lost close to half its value, an investment in Strategy nearly doubled. The resulting performance gap places Strategy ahead of all but a handful of its industry peers.

Was It Strategy's Industry?

No, though the S&P 500 index provided a lift. The S&P 500, dominated by the largest companies, rose 70.0% over the same five years. Strategy stock still finished ahead of the index.

The company's own industry operated as a drag. Among the 12 industries within the Information Technology sector, Application Software ranked 11th based on the typical company's five-year return. The typical technology stock also fell. Strategy rose against the tide of its own group.

What Did Strategy's Business Do?

Sales at Strategy remained flat. Revenue growth averaged 0.02% a year over the past three years, compared with 11.1% for the typical software company. Between 2021 and 2026, revenue slipped 1.7%.

Profit per share moved the wrong way, from a loss of $4.33 a share in the twelve months to June 2021 to a loss of $97.21 in the twelve months to June 2026. The operating margin shifted from a 14.3% profit in the twelve months to June 2021 to an 8.1% loss in the twelve months to June 2026. Over those same years, the diluted share count rose 261.7%, leaving each share with a smaller slice of a business that loses money. Strategy reported an $8.22 billion loss in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, compared with a $10.02 billion profit a year earlier, as the bitcoin price declined, the WSJ reported. Over the past year, the company's net loss amounted to more than 60 times its revenue.
